entities.summary:
Peter of Benevento was a prominent Italian canon lawyer and cardinal who played a significant role in the medieval papal legateship. Born into a noble family, he rose to prominence through his academic achievements and became a key figure in the development of canon law. In 1198, Pope Innocent III appointed him as the papal legate to the Holy Roman Empire, where he negotiated the Treaty of Venice, securing significant concessions for the Catholic Church.

 Peter's influence extended beyond his administrative duties, as he was also a prolific writer and commentator on legal matters. His treatises on canon law were widely read and respected throughout Europe, contributing significantly to the codification of ecclesiastical laws. Moreover, he was involved in the selection of several popes, including Pope Innocent III himself.

 Peter's legacy is marked by his enduring contributions to the development of canon law, as well as his notable role in shaping the politics and diplomacy of the medieval papacy. His influence can be seen in the subsequent appointments of prominent cardinals and bishops, who went on to play significant roles in European history.

 The most striking aspect of Peter's life was his untimely death in 1219, which left a power vacuum that would have far-reaching consequences for the Catholic Church. Despite this, his work remained widely respected, and he is remembered as one of the most influential figures in the development of medieval canon law.
